mainTopic: When an ox or a bed counts as an אהל, רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון on sleeping under a bed in the סוכה, and a סוכה supported by a bed.
overview: This amud opens with the end of רבא's worry that a child could become טמא from a קבר התהום. A ברייתא supports him: according to רבי יהודה, the children who drew water for the פרה אדומה rode directly on wide-bellied oxen, whose bodies served as an אהל. The גמרא asks how this fits with רבי יהודה sleeping under a bed in the סוכה, which shows he does not treat a bed as an אהל. Several answers are tried and rejected. רבא finally explains that an ox's body is made by nature to cover its insides. A second answer says that for רבי יהודה a temporary אהל like a bed cannot cancel the permanent סוכה, and רבי שמעון disagrees on exactly this point. The גמרא then explains רבי שמעון's lesson from the story of טבי, and notes that even the casual talk of תלמידי חכמים must be studied. A new משנה follows about a סוכה that rests on the legs of a bed, which רבי יהודה invalidates if it cannot stand on its own. Two אמוראים give different reasons for his ruling, and the גמרא shows the case where those reasons differ. אביי adds that if the roofing rests on poles attached to the bed, everyone agrees the סוכה is כשרה.

steps.title: End of רבא's statement about the danger of קבר התהום
steps.stepSummary: The closing words of רבא's statement from the previous section: the child could become טמא through a hidden grave deep underground.
steps.simpleTranslation: [...and he will become impure] through a grave in the depths.
steps.whatsHappening: These are just the final words of רבא's statement, which began on the previous amud. He is finishing his worry that a child could become טמא from a hidden grave underground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קבר התהום is a grave nobody knew about, buried deep in the ground. רבא's concern is that if any part of the child sticks out beyond the protective covering, he is no longer shielded from that hidden טומאה. The next step brings a ברייתא to support exactly this concern.

keyTerms.meaning: A grave hidden deep in the ground that no one knew about

phrases.english: through a grave in the depths.
phrases.notes: Tail end of רבא's statement earlier.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's statement begun on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A child who sticks out a limb beyond the covering can become טמא from קבר התהום.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבא: no doors, the children rode right on the oxen
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה teaches that doors were not used at all. The children sat directly on wide-bellied Egyptian oxen, holding stone cups, to draw water for the פרה אדומה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא in line with רבא: רבי יהודה says they would not bring doors at all. A child is overconfident, and he might stick out his head or a limb and become טמא from a קבר התהום. Instead they brought Egyptian oxen with wide bellies. The children sat on their backs holding stone cups. When they reached the שילוח, they got down and filled the cups, then climbed back up and sat on the oxen's backs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up רבא's worry. According to רבי יהודה, the children rode directly on the oxen with no doors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sitting on a big door makes a child feel safe, so he might lean out past the edge and lose his protection. Without doors, the wide belly of the ox itself served as the אהל shielding the child from the טומאה underground. The stone cups were used because stone does not become טמא.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא in support of him
He is overconfident and not careful
The Siloam spring in Jerusalem, where the water was drawn
Stone cups, which cannot become טמא

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up רבי יהודה's position that an ox's body counts as an אהל. The rest of this passage challenges exactly that point.

phrases.english: It is taught in accordance with Rava.
Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא הָיוּ מְבִיאִין דְּלָתוֹת כׇּל עִיקָּר,
phrases.english: They would not bring doors at all,

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁדַּעְתּוֹ שֶׁל תִּינוֹק גַּסָּה עָלָיו,
phrases.english: because a child is overconfident,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמָּא יוֹצִיא רֹאשׁוֹ אוֹ אֶחָד מֵאֵבָרָיו
phrases.english: perhaps he will stick out his head or one of his limbs
and become impure through a grave in the depths.
Rather, they would bring Egyptian oxen
whose bellies are wide,
and the children would sit on their backs,
with stone cups in their hands.
When they reached the Shiloach,
they got down and filled them,
and climbed up and sat themselves on their backs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא's concern with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's concern that a child might stick out a limb and become טמא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא quoting רבי יהודה: no doors were used, for this exact reason.

steps.title: Challenge from רבי יהודה sleeping under a bed
steps.stepSummary: A bed is several fistbreadths (אגרופים) high, yet רבי יהודה slept under it in the סוכה. That shows he does not treat a bed as an אהל, so why would an ox count as one?
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about a bed, which is several fists high? We learned in the משנה that רבי יהודה said: our custom was to sleep under the bed in front of the elders!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי יהודה's view by pointing to another statement of his in our own משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a bed counted as an אהל, sleeping under it would mean sleeping under a roof that blocks the סוכה, and the מצוה would not be fulfilled. רבי יהודה slept there, so he must hold that a bed is not an אהל. That seems to contradict his treating an ox's belly as an אהל.

keyTerms.meaning: And we learned in a משנה

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not about טומאה directly. It compares two cases where something either counts as an אהל or does not: a bed in the סוכה and an ox over קבר התהום.

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲרֵי מִטָּה, דְּיֵשׁ בָּהּ כַּמָּה אֶגְרוֹפִים,
phrases.english: But what about a bed, which is several fistbreadths high,
and we learned: Rabbi Yehuda says:
It was our custom that we would sleep
under the bed in front of the elders!

steps.triggerLanguage: וַהֲרֵי מִטָּה, דְּיֵשׁ בָּהּ כַּמָּה אֶגְרוֹפִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהודה's view in the ברייתא using his own statement in our משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's ruling that an ox's belly is an אהל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה does not treat a bed as an אהל, even though it is high enough. That contradicts treating an ox as one.

steps.title: A bed is different: it is made for use on top
steps.stepSummary: A bed's purpose is to be used on top of, not to cover what is under it, so it is not an אהל.
steps.simpleTranslation: A bed is different, since it is made for use on top of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by pointing out what makes a bed special.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something counts as an אהל when it serves as a covering. A bed's purpose is the space on top, where you lie down, so the space underneath does not count as covered.

keyTerms.meaning: Made for use on top of it

phrases.english: A bed is different,
since it is made for use on top of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the bed challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A bed should be an אהל like an ox, since both are tall enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: A bed is made to be used on top of, so it does not function as a covering.

steps.title: But oxen are also used on top
steps.stepSummary: Oxen are ridden and loaded on their backs, so the same reasoning should mean they are not an אהל either.
steps.simpleTranslation: Oxen too are made for use on top of them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the previous answer. Oxen are also used on their backs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If being used on top cancels the status of אהל, an ox should not count either, since its back is where people ride and load things. So the difference between a bed and an ox remains unexplained.

keyTerms.meaning: Made for use on their backs

phrases.english: Oxen too are made for use on top of them!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The distinction that a bed is made for use on top.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same is true of oxen, so the distinction fails.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: oxen shelter shepherds from sun and rain
steps.stepSummary: רבין reports רבי אלעזר's answer: oxen are different because shepherds take shelter under them from the sun and the rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבין came, he said in the name of רבי אלעזר: oxen are different, since they protect the shepherds from the sun on hot days and from the rain on rainy days.
steps.whatsHappening: A new answer arrives from ארץ ישראל to explain why oxen do count as an אהל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though oxen are used on top, people actually use the space underneath them as shelter. That real covering function is what makes them an אהל, unlike a bed.

keyTerms.meaning: When רבין came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: When Ravin came, he said that Rabbi Elazar said:
Oxen are different,
since they protect the shepherds
in the sun from the sun
and in the rain from the rain.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a new distinction after the first one failed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New distinction based on actual use as shelter
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Oxen are like beds, since both are used on top.
steps.terutzMaskana: Oxen are an אהל because people really shelter under them.

steps.title: But a bed also protects the shoes underneath
steps.stepSummary: If sheltering is the reason, a bed should also be an אהל, since it shelters shoes and sandals stored under it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, a bed too should count, since it protects the shoes and sandals underneath it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אלעזר's answer. A bed also shelters things. The next step answers this challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר made 'it shelters something' the reason for being an אהל. A bed does shelter something: the shoes kept under it. So the contradiction between the bed and the ox comes back, and the answer continues next.

phrases.english: If so, a bed too,

phrases.aramaic: הוֹאִיל וּמְגִינָּה עַל מִנְעָלִים וְסַנְדָּלִים שֶׁתַּחְתֶּיהָ!
phrases.english: since it protects the shoes and sandals underneath it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי אלעזר's distinction.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's reason that oxen are an אהל because they shelter.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A bed also shelters what is under it, so by that reason a bed should be an אהל too.

steps.title: רבא: An ox's body is built to shelter
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the shelter-for-shepherds answer and says oxen are different because their bodies are naturally made to cover and protect their insides, as a פסוק in איוב shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: Oxen are different, because their bodies are made to protect their insides, as the פסוק says: "With skin and flesh You clothed me, and with bones and sinews You covered me."
steps.whatsHappening: The previous answer, that shepherds take shelter under oxen, fell apart because a bed also shelters shoes. So רבא gives a brand-new reason why an ox counts as an אהל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא does not rely on what people happen to do with oxen. He points to what the ox's body is by nature: skin and flesh made to cover what is inside, the way a tent covers. A bed has no built-in covering role like that, so the comparison to a bed no longer works.

keyTerms.meaning: You covered me (same root as סוכה, 'covering/shelter')

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
phrases.notes: "אלא" signals that the earlier answer (shepherds' shelter) is dropped.

phrases.english: Oxen are different,
since they are made to protect
their own innards,
as it is stated: "With skin and flesh You have clothed me
and with bones and sinews You have covered me."
phrases.notes: תסוככני shares a root with סוכה. The body itself is described as a 'covering'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer from Step 6, which Step 7 knocked down, with a new reason based on the ox's nature.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New distinguishing reason (inherent nature of the object)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Oxen are an אהל because people shelter under them, which would make a bed an אהל too.
steps.terutzMaskana: Oxen are an אהל because their bodies are naturally a covering. A bed has no such built-in sheltering nature.

steps.title: A temporary covering cannot cancel a permanent סוכה
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the bed may be an אהל in general, but רבי יהודה holds that a סוכה must be a permanent dwelling, and a temporary covering like a bed cannot cancel a permanent one.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: רבי יהודה follows his own view, since he said a סוכה must be a permanent dwelling. So the bed is a temporary dwelling and the סוכה is a permanent tent, and a temporary tent cannot come and cancel a permanent tent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a completely different way to answer the question of why רבי יהודה slept under a bed. The answer is not about what makes something an אהל. It is about a special rule for סוכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer does not say a bed fails to be an אהל. It says that even if the bed is an אהל, it is only a temporary one, and it is too weak to override the permanent סוכה above it. So the bed case is an exception that applies inside a סוכה, while the oxen case stays as it was.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces an alternative answer)

steps.confusionAlert: This answer does NOT claim that a bed is not an אהל. It accepts that a bed may be an אהל but says a temporary אהל cannot cancel a permanent סוכה.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
Rabbi Yehuda follows his own reasoning,
for he said: we require a sukkah to be a permanent dwelling.
So the bed is a temporary dwelling,
and the sukkah is a permanent tent
and a temporary tent does not come
and cancel a permanent tent.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה לְטַעְמֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, independent answer to the question from Step 3, separate from רבא's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (the bed case is special to סוכה)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If רבי יהודה slept under a bed, he must hold that a bed is not an אהל at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: A bed may be an אהל, but a temporary אהל cannot cancel a permanent סוכה according to רבי יהודה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the core disagreement between רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון about sleeping under a bed in the סוכה.

steps.title: But רבי שמעון also requires a permanent סוכה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the alternative answer: רבי שמעון also says a סוכה must be permanent, yet he holds that a temporary covering does cancel it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי שמעון also says a סוכה must be a permanent dwelling, and still, a temporary tent comes and cancels the permanent tent!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the logic of the last answer. If requiring a permanent סוכה automatically meant a bed cannot cancel it, then רבי שמעון, who requires the same thing, should agree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous step tied the 'temporary cannot cancel permanent' rule to the view that a סוכה must be permanent. רבי שמעון holds that view too, but he rules that sleeping under a bed does not count. So the link between the two ideas seems broken.

phrases.english: But Rabbi Shimon, who also says
we require a sukkah to be a permanent dwelling,
(behold) a temporary tent does come
phrases.notes: The parenthetical word is a textual variant in the printed edition.

phrases.english: and cancel a permanent tent!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning of Step 9's alternative answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 9 that requiring a permanent סוכה explains why a bed cannot cancel it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי שמעון shares the premise (permanent סוכה) but reaches the opposite conclusion (a bed does cancel it), so the premise alone cannot produce the conclusion.

steps.title: Yes, that is exactly their disagreement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the point: both require a permanent סוכה, but they argue over whether a temporary covering can cancel a permanent one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, this is what they disagree about. One Sage holds that a temporary tent can cancel a permanent tent, and the other Sage holds that a temporary tent cannot cancel a permanent tent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by admitting that requiring a permanent סוכה is not enough to settle the case. There is a separate disagreement about temporary versus permanent coverings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate ideas. Both Sages agree that a סוכה must be permanent. They argue about the second idea: רבי שמעון says a temporary covering can override a permanent one, and רבי יהודה says it cannot.

phrases.english: (Yes,) in this they disagree:
One Sage holds:

phrases.aramaic: אָתֵי אֹהֶל עֲרַאי וּמְבַטֵּל אֹהֶל קֶבַע,
phrases.english: a temporary tent comes and cancels a permanent tent,
and the other Sage holds:

phrases.aramaic: לָא אָתֵי אֹהֶל עֲרַאי וּמְבַטֵּל אֹהֶל קֶבַע.
phrases.english: a temporary tent does not come and cancel a permanent tent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by locating the disagreement on a separate principle.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying the true point of dispute
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Requiring a permanent סוכה automatically means a temporary covering cannot cancel it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The two ideas are independent. Both Sages require a permanent סוכה, but they disagree over whether a temporary אהל can cancel a permanent one.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה: a temporary אהל (like a bed) cannot cancel the permanent סוכה, so sleeping under a bed is fine. רבי שמעון: a temporary אהל does cancel it, so sleeping under a bed does not count.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: the incident with טבי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words about רבי שמעון's story of טבי, the slave of רבן גמליאל, to begin explaining it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון said: There was an incident with טבי, his slave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה and quotes it. This is a setup line that prepares for the ברייתא explaining what רבי שמעון learned from the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, טבי slept under a bed in the סוכה, and רבן גמליאל explained that טבי knew slaves are exempt from סוכה. The quote marks the topic the גמרא is about to explain.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident, a story with legal weight

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon said:
There was an incident with Tavi, his slave.
phrases.notes: טבי was the slave of רבן גמליאל.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּטָבִי עַבְדּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the רבי יהודה / רבי שמעון dispute to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Quotation of the משנה's line introducing the story of טבי.

steps.title: Two lessons from רבן גמליאל's words
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records that רבי שמעון learned two laws from רבן גמליאל's remark: slaves are exempt from סוכה, and someone who sleeps under a bed has not fulfilled the מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי שמעון said: From what רבן גמליאל said, we learned two things. We learned that slaves are exempt from סוכה, and we learned that one who sleeps under the bed has not fulfilled his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that spells out what רבי שמעון learned from the story of טבי. This explains why the story supports his view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל praised טבי for sleeping under the bed because טבי knew slaves are exempt. That only makes sense if sleeping under a bed does not count as being in the סוכה. So the story gives both laws at once: slaves are exempt, and sleeping under a bed does not fulfill the obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי שמעון, the story of טבי proves two laws: עבדים are exempt from סוכה, and someone sleeping under a bed in the סוכה has not fulfilled the מצוה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how a casual remark of a great Sage can serve as a source for practical הלכה.

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Shimon said:
From the conversation of Rabban Gamliel
we learned two things:
we learned that slaves are exempt from the sukkah,
and we learned that one who sleeps beneath the bed
has not fulfilled his obligation.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: מִשִּׂיחָתוֹ שֶׁל רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the story quoted in Step 12 by showing what רבי שמעון derived from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Slaves are exempt from סוכה, and one who sleeps under a bed in the סוכה has not fulfilled his obligation.

steps.title: Why say 'conversation' instead of 'words'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the wording of the ברייתא: why did רבי שמעון say he learned from רבן גמליאל's 'conversation' and not simply from his 'words'?
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say: 'From the words of רבן גמליאל'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the wording of the ברייתא from the previous step. The usual phrase would be 'from the words of רבן גמליאל', so why did it say 'from his conversation'?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said רבי שמעון learned two laws 'מִשִּׂיחָתוֹ', from his casual talk. The normal phrase for learning a law is 'מִדְּבָרָיו', from his words. The גמרא assumes an unusual word must be teaching something extra.

keyTerms.meaning: And let him say (a challenge to the wording)
The נשיא, whose remark about טבי is being discussed

phrases.english: And let him say: 'From the words of Rabban Gamliel'?
phrases.notes: The ברייתא actually said 'from his conversation' (מִשִּׂיחָתוֹ).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the exact wording of the ברייתא quoted in Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'from the conversation of רבן גמליאל' in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The standard expression would be 'from his words', so the unusual wording seems to need a reason.

steps.title: Even the casual talk of scholars must be studied
steps.stepSummary: The word 'conversation' teaches a side lesson: even the everyday talk of תלמידי חכמים deserves careful study. This is learned from the פסוק 'its leaf does not wither'.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us something in passing. As רב אחא בר אדא said, and some say it was רב אחא בר אדא quoting רב המנונא quoting רב: From where do we know that even the casual conversation of תלמידי חכמים needs study? Because it says 'and its leaf does not wither'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא chose the word 'conversation' on purpose. It is teaching that even casual remarks of תלמידי חכמים contain Torah worth learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל was only chatting about his slave, and yet two laws were learned from it. רב finds this idea in תהלים: a צדיק is like a tree whose fruit, and even whose leaves, are valuable. The 'fruit' is a scholar's formal teaching, and the 'leaves' are his casual talk.

keyTerms.meaning: A lesson taught in passing, on the side
The casual talk of Torah scholars
'And its leaf does not wither' (תהלים א:ג)

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא said 'conversation' on purpose: even the casual words of תלמידי חכמים are Torah and should be studied.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the discussion of the טבי story. It also gives a lasting principle: the everyday behavior and speech of תלמידי חכמים are a source of הלכה.

phrases.aramaic: מִילְּתָא אַגַּב אוֹרְחֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן,
phrases.english: It teaches us a matter in passing,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּאָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר אַדָּא,
phrases.english: like that which Rav Acha bar Adda said,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר אַדָּא
phrases.english: and some say: Rav Acha bar Adda said
phrases.notes: The second version gives a longer chain of who quoted whom.

phrases.english: that Rav Hamnuna said that Rav said:
From where do we know that even the conversation of Torah scholars
requires study?
As it is stated: 'And its leaf does not wither.'
phrases.notes: Leaves are the less important part of the tree, like casual talk, and they are valuable too.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִילְּתָא אַגַּב אוֹרְחֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording challenge of Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the unusual wording as deliberately teaching an extra lesson
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'conversation' seemed out of place for learning הלכה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word was chosen to teach that even the casual talk of scholars must be studied, based on 'וְעָלֵהוּ לֹא יִבּוֹל'.

steps.title: New משנה: a סוכה resting on bed legs
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that a סוכה whose roof is supported by the legs of a bed is כשרה. רבי יהודה says that if it cannot stand on its own, it is פסולה.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who rests his סוכה on the legs of a bed, it is כשרה. רבי יהודה says: if it cannot stand by itself, it is פסולה.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. Someone uses the posts of a bed to hold up the roof of his סוכה. The תנא קמא says it is כשרה, and רבי יהודה says it is פסולה if the סוכה would fall without the bed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the bed is used as a support, not as a covering. That makes this a different issue from sleeping under a bed. The argument is whether a סוכה that depends on a bed for support is still valid.

keyTerms.meaning: משנה: the opening of a new משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the earlier case of sleeping under a bed. There the bed was a covering that blocked the סכך. Here the bed is a support that holds the סכך up.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
One who supports his sukkah on the legs of the bed, it is valid.
Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: אִם אֵינָהּ יְכוֹלָה לַעֲמוֹד בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָהּ — פְּסוּלָה.
phrases.english: If it cannot stand on its own, it is invalid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic after the טבי discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A סוכה supported by bed legs is כשרה. According to רבי יהודה it is פסולה if it cannot stand without the bed.

steps.title: What is רבי יהודה's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יהודה invalidates a סוכה that depends on the bed.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is the reason of רבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion by asking for the reasoning behind רבי יהודה's ruling. This sets up the next step, where two answers are given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave רבי יהודה's ruling but not his reason. Knowing the reason tells us which other cases his ruling applies to.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא who invalidates the סוכה

phrases.english: GEMARA:
What is the reason of Rabbi Yehuda?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind רבי יהודה's ruling in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason רבי יהודה invalidates a סוכה supported by a bed

steps.title: Two explanations: not permanent, or held up by something that can become טמא
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא and רבי אבא בר ממל disagree. One says the סוכה lacks permanence. The other says it is held up by an object that can become טמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא and רבי אבא בר ממל argue about it. One says: because it has no permanence. The other says: because he holds it up with something that can become טמא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two different reasons for רבי יהודה's ruling, from two אמוראים. We are not told which אמורא said which reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reason one: a bed can be moved, so a סוכה that leans on it could collapse, and it is not a stable dwelling. Reason two: a bed is a כלי that can become טמא. This view holds that not only the סכך but also what holds it up must be something that cannot become טמא.

keyTerms.meaning: He holds it up, supports it
An object that can become ritually impure

steps.whyThisMatters: The second reason introduces an important idea: the rule about סכך might also apply to what holds the סכך up (מעמיד).

phrases.aramaic: פְּלִיגִי בַּהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא וְרַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר מֶמֶל.
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Abba bar Memel disagree about it.

phrases.aramaic: חַד אָמַר: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁאֵין לָהּ קֶבַע.
phrases.english: One said: because it has no permanence.
And one said: because he supports it
with an object that is susceptible to ritual impurity.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּלִיגִי בַּהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא וְרַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר מֶמֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 17 with two competing reasons.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Either the סוכה lacks permanence, or it is supported by a מקבל טומאה object.

steps.title: What is the practical difference between the two reasons?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks in what case the two explanations would lead to different rulings.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: Since a bed is both movable and able to become טמא, both reasons give the same result for a bed. The גמרא asks for a case where they would disagree, and the next step gives that case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a bed, both reasons invalidate the סוכה. So the גמרא looks for a case that separates the two ideas.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the practical difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a case that separates the two reasons given in Step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where the two reasons for רבי יהודה give different rulings

steps.title: The case of iron skewers
steps.stepSummary: If someone sticks iron skewers into the ground and puts סכך on them, the 'permanence' view says it is כשרה. The 'טומאה' view says it is פסולה.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, where he stuck iron skewers into the ground and put סכך on them. According to the one who says the problem is lack of permanence, this has permanence. According to the one who says the problem is supporting with something that can become טמא, here he is supporting it with something that can become טמא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the case that shows the difference: iron skewers stuck firmly in the ground holding up the סכך. One reason makes this סוכה כשרה, and the other makes it פסולה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Skewers driven into the ground are fixed and stable, so the 'permanence' problem is gone. But iron skewers are כלים that can become טמא, so the 'מעמיד' problem is still there. The case separates the two reasons cleanly.

keyTerms.meaning: He stuck (it) firmly into the ground
According to the one who said

steps.whatToRemember: Iron skewers in the ground are permanent but can become טמא. So they are כשר according to the 'קבע' reason and פסול according to the 'מקבל טומאה' reason.

phrases.english: For example, where he stuck iron skewers into the ground
and placed roofing on them.

phrases.aramaic: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לְפִי שֶׁאֵין לָהּ קֶבַע —
phrases.english: According to the one who said it is because it has no permanence,
here it has permanence (so it is valid).
And the one who said it is because he supports it
with an object susceptible to impurity,
here he supports it with an object susceptible to impurity (so it is invalid).

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּגוֹן שֶׁנָּעַץ שַׁפּוּדִין שֶׁל בַּרְזֶל וְסִיכֵּךְ עֲלֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 19 by giving the case that separates the two reasons.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Iron skewers fixed in the ground: כשר by the קבע reason, פסול by the מקבל טומאה reason.

steps.title: אביי limits the dispute to roofing that leans on the bed
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the argument in the משנה is only about a case where the סכך leans on the bed. If the סכך is placed on top of the bed (on poles attached to it), everyone agrees the סוכה is כשרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: They only taught this dispute where one leaned the roofing on the bed. But if one put the roofing on top of the bed, the סוכה is fit.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי makes a new statement that narrows the case of the משנה. He says רבי יהודה's ruling of פסול only covers one specific setup.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to build with a bed. In 'סמך' the bed's legs themselves hold up the roofing. In 'סיכך על גב המטה' poles are fixed onto the bed and the roofing rests on those poles. אביי says only the first case is under dispute. In the second case even רבי יהודה agrees it is כשרה.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught [this] about... (a formula that limits a ruling to one case)
He leaned/supported: the roofing rests directly on the bed
He placed roofing: here, on poles attached to the bed

steps.confusionAlert: 'על גב המטה' does not mean the סכך lies directly on the bed. It means poles are fastened to the bed, and the סכך sits on those poles. The bed is not what directly holds the roof.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא סָמַךְ.
phrases.english: Abaye said: They only taught [the dispute] where he leaned [the roofing on the bed].
phrases.notes: The bed's legs are the direct support.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל סִיכֵּךְ עַל גַּב הַמִּטָּה — כְּשֵׁרָה.
phrases.english: But if he placed the roofing atop the bed, it is fit.
phrases.notes: Poles fixed to the bed hold the roofing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא סָמַךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the גמרא explained both reasons for רבי יהודה (steps 18 to 20), אביי narrows the exact case where his ruling of פסול applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה's ruling of פסול applies only when the סכך leans directly on the bed. If the סכך rests on poles attached to the bed, everyone agrees the סוכה is כשרה.

steps.title: Why is the roofing on top of the bed fit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason the second setup is כשרה even according to רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next step. It wants to know why אביי's case is כשרה under both explanations from step 18.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two different explanations for רבי יהודה's ruling. So the גמרא must show that the 'on top of the bed' case avoids both problems. Otherwise one of the two views might still say it is פסולה.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind אביי's limitation in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the סוכה whose סכך rests on poles fixed to the bed is כשרה according to both explanations of רבי יהודה.

steps.title: It works according to both explanations
steps.stepSummary: Under the 'no קבע' view, this סוכה does have קבע. Under the 'held up by something that can become טמא' view, the bed is not what holds it up.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who said it is unfit because it lacks permanence, here it has permanence. According to the one who said it is unfit because he holds it up with something that can become impure, here he does not hold it up with something that can become impure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by going through both explanations from step 18. It shows that neither problem exists in אביי's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the קבע view: the poles are fixed to the bed, so if the bed moves the roof moves with it and does not fall. That makes the סוכה stable. For the טומאה view: the roof rests on the poles, not on the bed itself. So the direct support is not something that can become טמא.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who said...
He holds it up / supports it
An object that can become ritually impure (like a bed)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה only invalidates a סוכה when the bed itself directly holds up the roofing. If poles fixed to the bed hold the roofing, the סוכה is כשרה according to everyone. It has קבע, and its direct support is not something that can become טמא.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common method in the גמרא. A limitation of a ruling is checked against every explanation of that ruling, to prove it holds under each one.

phrases.aramaic: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לְפִי שֶׁאֵין לָהּ קֶבַע —
phrases.english: According to the one who said [it is unfit] because it has no permanence,
here it does have permanence.
phrases.notes: If the bed moves, the roof moves with it and does not collapse.

phrases.english: According to the one who said [it is unfit] because he supports it
with an object that can become impure,
here he does not support it
with an object that can become impure.
phrases.notes: The poles, not the bed, hold up the roofing.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לְפִי שֶׁאֵין לָהּ קֶבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22 by applying both explanations from step 18 to אביי's case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Under the קבע view, the סוכה is stable because the roof moves together with the bed. Under the טומאה view, the direct support is the poles, not the bed.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: סיכך על גב המטה is כשרה according to both explanations. The dispute is limited to סמך.
